newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - To take or not to take out 6.40.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - To take or not to take out 6.40.

text.p: The U.S. credit market has already priced in the best U.S. economic scenario there is and will need the confirmation of such hopes -- and more -- to break through important technical levels, analysts said.
The credit market soared to pricey levels on Monday, propped up by an ever-rallying dollar, lower-than-expected Treasury borrowing needs, and talk of an imminent balanced-budget agreement.
This forced the 30-year bond yield down to 6.40 percent, a significant hurdle in the past.
The long bond gained 22/32 to 102.29/30 while the 10-year note rose 12/32 to 103/19/20, yielding 6.13 percent.

"Taking out 6.40 percent (bond yield) won't be all that easy," predicted Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A. who noted that the last bond rally bottomed out with "the lowest closing yield in December 1996 at 6.35 percent."

Traders said the market was taking something of a gamble by rallying in front of an important economic report, mainly one known to be closely watched by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan -- the Employment Cost Index.
The second-quarter ECI is due out at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.
The consensus in a Reuters survey expected the ECI to be reported at up 0.8 percent following a 0.6-percent increase in the first quarter.

"If the number comes out in line with the consensus forecast, this would leave the ECI year-over-year rate just under that important 3.0-percent threshold," Stiles said. "A higher-than-expected number, like up 1.0 percent, would be a big problem for the market."
A 3.0-percent annual increase in U.S. employment costs would not be cause for too much concern since inflation is also running at about that level, analysts said.

However, an acceleration in employment costs would likely trigger a Treasuries sell-off since this would revive fears of wage-driven inflation -- a phenomenon witnessed only to often late in the cycle of previous U.S. expansions, they added.

Another report set for release on Tuesday, at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT, is the Conference Board's Consumer Confidence Index for July, expected to merely confirm Americans' optimism. The consensus forecast is for a reading of 130.4 which would top the 28-year high set in June at 129.6.
Traders said the problem for Treasuries on Tuesday is that a lot of good news were priced in on Monday.
"The market responded to three positive factors, first the strong dollar. Second was Treasury's lower borrowings needs and third, prospects of a balanced-budget agreement," Stiles explained.

Propped up by lasting concern over the European single currency, the dollar surged to 1.8490 marks, its highest since November 1989. Also, Treasury said it would need to borrow $10 billion only in the July-September quarter -- half of most forecasts and the smallest shortfall since the late 1970s.
Both Congress and the White House sent word that they were nearing an agreement to balance the federal budget by 2002.
Other U.S. reports that may weigh on Treasuries this week are the second-quarter Gross Domestic Product, set for release on Thursday, and the July jobs data on Friday.

The Reuters consensus forecast expected a 1.9-percent rise after the sizzling 5.9-percent rate of the first quarter. For the payrolls due out on Friday, analysts predicted a 193,000 rise following June's 217,000 gain, while the unemployment rate would edge down to 4.9 percent from 5.0 percent.
The federal funds rate is seen opening on Tuesday near its target of 5.50 percent.
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1666 ))
